questions.stem: A genetic diagram shows parents Bb x Bb. A student writes the gametes as 'Bb' for each parent. What mistake has the student made?

options.text: The gametes should be written as 'BB' and 'bb'
Each gamete should contain only one allele, so the gametes are 'B' and 'b' from each parent
The gametes should be written as 'B' from one parent and 'b' from the other
There is no mistake; gametes contain both alleles

questions.explanation: During meiosis, alleles separate so each gamete contains only one allele from each gene. A parent with genotype Bb produces two types of gametes: those with B and those with b. Writing 'Bb' as a gamete is incorrect because it implies the gamete is diploid. This is a very common error in genetic diagrams at GCSE.

questions.stem: A family pedigree shows that two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis (a recessive condition). What are the genotypes of both parents?

options.text: One parent is CC and the other is Cc
One parent is Cc and the other is cc

questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is recessive (cc). For an affected child to be born, it must inherit a recessive allele from EACH parent. Since both parents are unaffected, they cannot be cc. They must each carry one recessive allele hidden by a dominant allele, making them both Cc (carriers). Only Cc x Cc can produce an affected child (cc) while both parents appear unaffected.

questions.stem: In a genetic diagram, a cross between Rr x Rr produces the following offspring: RR, Rr, Rr, rr. A student says 'This means exactly 3 out of every 4 children will be red.' Why is this statement misleading?

options.text: The 3:1 ratio is a probability, not a guarantee; actual results may differ due to the random nature of fertilisation
The ratio only applies to plants, not animals
All four offspring should be red because R is dominant

questions.explanation: The 3:1 ratio represents the probability (expected ratio), not a guaranteed outcome. Each offspring independently has a 3/4 chance of being red and 1/4 chance of being white. With small numbers, actual results often deviate from the expected ratio by chance. The predicted ratio becomes more accurate with larger numbers of offspring.

questions.stem: A Punnett square for tongue rolling ability (T = can roll, t = cannot roll) shows cross Tt x tt. What percentage of offspring are expected to be unable to roll their tongue?
questions.explanation: The Punnett square for Tt x tt gives offspring: Tt, Tt, tt, tt. Two out of four offspring (50%) have the genotype tt and cannot roll their tongue. Two out of four (50%) have the genotype Tt and can roll their tongue. This 1:1 ratio occurs whenever a heterozygous individual is crossed with a homozygous recessive individual.

questions.stem: When constructing a genetic diagram for an exam, which of the following should always be included for full marks?

options.text: Parental phenotypes, parental genotypes, gametes, Punnett square, offspring genotypes, and offspring phenotype ratio
Just the parental genotypes and the offspring ratio
A drawing of the chromosomes and the DNA sequence

questions.explanation: A complete genetic diagram for GCSE should show: parental phenotypes (what they look like), parental genotypes (e.g., Bb x Bb), gametes (shown in circles, e.g., B and b), a Punnett square showing all possible offspring combinations, offspring genotypes (e.g., BB, Bb, Bb, bb), and the phenotype ratio (e.g., 3 brown : 1 white). Missing any step can cost marks.
